title: OpenGreenIoT Device Spec
description: Schema for OpenGreenIoT device specification files (BLE and WiFi). Permissive by design: unknown keys are allowed so bespoke, device-specific metadata (e.g. protobuf/state_machine blocks) can travel alongside the standard fields. Consumers (the Flutter+Rust mobile app, Home Assistant) parse the subset they understand and ignore the rest.

allOf.$comment: A device spec must document at least one access surface, otherwise it says nothing a consumer can act on. Reference specs (device.type starting with 'reference-') are exempt: they document a published protocol — SAE J1979 PIDs, ISO 14229 UDS services, ISO 15765-2 framing — that other specs cite instead of restating, and so carry protocol tables rather than an access surface of their own. `camera` counts (a live feed is an access surface), and an `integration: identify_only` device counts when it carries a `discovery` block — for it the access surface IS 'find it and hand the user to its admin page', which is the whole point of an identify-only entry.

A reference spec is not a device, so it must not claim a device category — and a device must not claim to be a reference. `type` starting with 'reference-' and `category: reference` are two spellings of the same fact, and the schema keys the access-surface exemption above off the first one; letting them disagree would put a protocol table in the app's scan list wearing a light-bulb icon, or a real light bar in a consumer's list of published standards. Both directions are enforced here rather than only in this repository's pytest conventions, because the schema is published for standalone consumers who never run those tests.

hex_bytes.description: Space-separated hex byte sequence, e.g. '22 F1 90'. A '??' byte is an unknown/placeholder position. Automotive traces are conventionally written this way, so OBD payloads use hex strings rather than the integer arrays used for BLE writes.

can_id.description: CAN identifier in hex, e.g. '0x7E0' (11-bit) or '0x18DAF110' (29-bit).

obd_capability.description: One adapter capability. Requests declare what they need (`requires`) and adapters declare what they provide (`adapter_profile.capabilities`), so a consumer can decide up front whether a given dongle can run a given command instead of failing halfway through. single_frame: payloads of 7 bytes or fewer. multiframe_rx/tx: ISO 15765-2 segmentation in each direction — transmit is where clone firmware fails; some adapters expose it as a long-message mode (the UniCarScan UCSI-2100 accepts payloads up to 255 bytes where a stock ELM327 stops at 8). flow_control: client-supplied flow control (ATFCSH/ATFCSD/ATFCSM). custom_headers: arbitrary request/filter IDs (ATSH/ATCRA). raw_frames: auto-formatting off (ATCAF0), client does its own ISO-TP. monitor_all: passive bus sniffing (ATMA). alt_can_bus: manufacturer CAN buses on non-standard pins or wiring — Ford MS-CAN (medium-speed) and GM SW-CAN (single-wire), which tools such as FORScan need for body and chassis modules. non_standard_bitrate: buses outside the legislated OBD-II rates.

diagnostic_description.description: Reference to a vendor ECU-description file — a BMW/EDIABAS SGBD (.prg) or group file (.grp), an ODX/PDX container, a CDD, an A2L or a CAN database. These files are the authoritative definition of a module's jobs, results, addressing and scaling, so naming the exact file lets a consumer look the definition up instead of relying only on what we recovered by hand. NOTE: reference these files, never ship them — they are vendor copyright. Record where a licensed copy comes from in `source`.

type.description: File format. 'sgbd-prg' is a compiled BMW/EDIABAS ECU description (KOMBI.prg); 'sgbd-grp' is the group file that dispatches to the right variant (D_MOTOR.grp).

name.description: Filename as the vendor toolchain names it, e.g. 'KOMBI.prg'.

group.description: For an sgbd-prg, the .grp group file that selects it. Group files are the entry point when the exact variant is not known up front.

variant.description: ECU variant this description covers, when one group spans several.

sha256.description: Checksum of the exact file the facts here were derived from, so a consumer can tell whether it is looking at the same one.

source.description: Where a licensed copy is obtained (e.g. an EDIABAS/INPA/ISTA installation, a vendor tool bundle). Not a download link for redistributed vendor files.

provides.description: What this file authoritatively defines for the module.

mac_prefix_confidence.description:
How much of this block belongs to this device, and therefore how much weight a consumer may put on an address matching it. An OUI identifies whoever bought the block, so the honest answer is usually not 'high'.

'low' (the default, and what a bare string prefix means): the block is shared. Either IEEE subdivided it into MA-M/MA-S assignments held by unrelated companies -- C4:7C:8D covers fifteen -- or the address comes off a third-party radio module, so the block names a chip vendor rather than this product. A consumer should rank on it and nothing else.

'medium': the block genuinely belongs to this manufacturer, but covers their whole catalogue. Seeing it means 'something this vendor made', not 'this device'.

'high': the block is used by this device family and effectively nothing else -- a small vendor with a single product line, or an assignment observed only on this hardware. Rare, and it needs evidence in `notes`; the failure mode of guessing here is an app telling somebody it found a device they do not own.

verification.description: How much weight this fact carries. 'confirmed' = observed in our own capture or read back from the device; 'reported' = stated by vendor/community documentation but not reproduced here; 'hypothesis' = inferred and not yet tested. Anything not 'confirmed' must not be executed against a vehicle without review.

number_semantics.$comment: Shared vocabulary for what a numeric wire value MEANS, composed via allOf into every place a spec carries one: BLE command `parameters`, BLE characteristic `format` fields, `bus` message fields, and `payload_formats` fields. The OBD blocks keep their own `unit`/`scale`/`formula` trio because a decode-only `formula` can express non-linear scalings — but a formula cannot be run backwards, and command parameters must be ENCODED, so this block is deliberately linear (value = raw * scale + value_offset) and therefore invertible. A number whose meaning cannot be stated in these terms gets the linear part here and the rest in prose.

allOf.$comment: A unit that follows a device setting is only decodable if the spec says where to learn the setting; without that, 'device_setting' is a warning with no exit.

unit.description: Unit of the DECODED value, after `scale` and `value_offset` are applied: 'C', 'F', '%', 'km/h', 'rpm', 'ms'. This states what is ON THE WIRE, not what the device happens to display — the Ember Mug always encodes centi-degrees C even when its screen shows Fahrenheit, so its temperature fields say 'C' and the display preference is a separate characteristic. Omit for dimensionless values (a raw brightness step, an enumerated code).

scale.description: Multiplier applied to the raw value to get `unit`: value = raw * scale (+ `value_offset`). Absent means 1. Same convention as the OBD blocks' `scale`. For a command parameter the client encodes by inverting: raw = round((value - value_offset) / scale).

value_offset.description: Additive term applied after `scale`: value = raw * scale + value_offset. Absent means 0. Named value_offset because bare `offset` already means a byte position in `format` and `bus` fields. Present because most real scalings carry an offset — the automotive 'x - 40' idiom, or the Gerbing heat controller's temperature (value = raw * 0.5 + 85 in F) — and reducing such a conversion to a bare multiplier silently drops the offset and yields a wrong reading.

unit_source.description: Whether the wire unit is a constant of the protocol ('fixed', the default) or follows a device setting ('device_setting'). Both patterns are common in temperature devices and confusing them corrupts every reading: the Ember Mug is 'fixed' (always centi-C; its C/F characteristic changes only the display), while the Inkbird iBBQ transmits raw numbers in whichever unit the device is currently set to — the same raw 165 means 165 C or 165 F depending on state, so a client must check before decoding. When 'device_setting', name where the active unit is learned in `unit_reference`, map the setting's values in `unit_values`, and use `unit` (if present) for the device's out-of-box default.

unit_reference.description: Where a client learns the active unit when `unit_source` is 'device_setting': the name of the `format` field, command or message that carries it, qualified as 'characteristic_uuid.field_name' or 'message_name.field_name' where a bare name would be ambiguous. Required with unit_source 'device_setting'.

unit_values.description: Map from the referenced unit-setting's raw value to the unit then in force, e.g. {0: 'C', 1: 'F'}. The key 'default' covers every unlisted value — the Inkbird unit byte means F when 0x46 (ASCII 'F') and C for anything else, which is {0x46: 'F', default: 'C'}.

values.description: Meaning of each raw value, for numbers that are really enumerated codes: {0: 'standby', 1: 'empty', 2: 'filling'}. The machine-readable sibling of the free-text `encoding` on `bus` fields and the `values` table in `payload_formats`. A field carrying `values` is a code table — `unit` and `scale` rarely apply, and a consumer should render the labels rather than the number.

title.description: Human title for the link. Use the page or video title when it is clear; otherwise write the shortest label that tells a reader why to open it.

url.description: HTTP(S) URL only. These links are for human follow-up, so verify they resolve before adding them; a dead link is worse than no link.

description.description: Why this reference is useful for this device. Do not make the reader guess whether a link is a teardown, a protocol write-up, vendor documentation, forum evidence, or a working implementation.

initialization.description: Ordered handshake / setup steps executed after connecting and before normal commands. Allowed at the top level and per-service.

characteristic.description: Target characteristic UUID for this step.

write.description: Byte sequence to write in this step.

read.description: If true, read from the characteristic in this step (e.g. to capture a handshake response / encryption key).

delay_ms.description: Delay in milliseconds to wait after this step.

encryption.description: Declares that a characteristic's payload is encrypted and how to derive the key.

algorithm.description: Symmetric cipher/mode used for this characteristic's payload.

key_derivation.description: How the key is obtained: a fixed static key, established via a connection handshake, or derived per device.

static_key.description: Hex-encoded static key, present only when key_derivation is 'static'.

setup_step.description: One ordered step in a provisioning or reset procedure, written so a consumer can render it as a wizard page or execute it directly.

action.description: Short imperative description of the step (e.g. 'Join the device setup AP').

actor.description: Who performs the step: the human ('user', e.g. pressing a button), the controlling app ('client'), or the device itself ('device', e.g. rebooting).

request.description: Protocol call this step issues, when the step is machine-executable.

service.description: Service URN, GATT service UUID, or API namespace.

action.description: SOAP action, HTTP path, or GATT message name.

expect.description: Observable success signal for this step (LED pattern, response value, state transition).

timeout_seconds.description: How long a consumer should wait for this step to complete before treating it as failed.

payload_formats.description: How to parse payloads that are not self-describing, keyed by the value's name (e.g. MetaInfo, ApList, InsightParams). Keyed by name rather than invented per-device keys so a consumer finds payload documentation the same way for every device. Allowed wherever payloads are returned: on a setup method, and at the top level alongside a device's control surface.

delimiter.description:
Separator, when the payload is several fields packed into one string: `fields[].index` then counts positions between occurrences of it.

This is the machine-readable half of what `parse_rules` says in prose, and it exists because prose is not something a decoder can follow. "Split on '|' and take field 0" was the documented rule for Wemo's BinaryState for as long as the format has been written down, and every consumer either hardcoded it per device or got a plausible wrong answer: read whole, `8|1492338954|…` is not a number, and a client that gives up there shows a live plug as off. Omit for a payload that is the whole value.

fields.description: Positional or named fields within the payload. Numeric fields may carry the shared number-semantics vocabulary (`unit`, `scale`, `value_offset`, …) — an InsightParams power column is milliwatts, and that belongs in data rather than prose.

values.description: Meaning of each value, for enumerated payloads.

parse_rules.description: Ordered, unambiguous parsing instructions. Spell out the traps: header lines to skip, trailing separators, columns that must be located from the end rather than by index, fields firmware may append.

example.description: A literal payload. Keep it real enough to test against — it is what an implementer will parse first.

framing.description: Structured packet framing applied on top of raw BLE writes for this characteristic. When `scheme` is set, every logical packet (including the byte sequences produced by this characteristic's `commands`) MUST be wrapped in the named fragment framing before it is written — the packet templates deliberately do NOT include the framing bytes.

length_prefix.description: Whether each frame is prefixed with its length.

checksum.description: Checksum algorithm appended to each frame.

max_chunk_size.description: Maximum payload bytes per frame (e.g. for chunked image uploads).

scheme.description: Named fragmentation scheme wrapping every logical packet written to (or notified by) this characteristic. `seeblue_envelope` (LEDGlow/SEEBlue motorcycle lighting): each write is [0x95][message_length u8][message_index u8][protocol_id u8][packet bytes][checksum u8], where message_length counts message_index through the last packet byte, message_index is a per-connection sequence number the client owns, protocol_id comes from the command's `protocol_id`, and the checksum is the 8-bit two's complement of message_length through the last packet byte. Protocol ids: 0x00 INTERNAL (post-connect auth handshake), 0x01 LIGHTING, 0x02 RESPONSE (the device answers on this one), 0x03 BOOTLOADER (latent OTA: flashes an Intel HEX over BLE; no firmware HEX is public), 0x04 GENERIC, 0x10 LEDGlow snapshot and the v2 UI-change commands. `daniao_fragment` (Hangzhou Daniao DDP/DNX platform): each BLE write/notification carries a 4-byte header [packet serial u8][total fragments u8][fragments remaining after this one u8, counting down to 0][channel tag u8] followed by up to (ATT payload - 4) packet bytes; reassembly keys on the first three bytes, and a single-fragment packet is [serial, 0x01, 0x00, tag] + packet. The device honors only the first write of a bulk (tag != 0) transfer, so each such packet must fit one write. VERIFIED on hardware (JY25CUT curtain controller, 2026-08-08): the controller silently ignores unframed writes and answers framed ones.

channel_tag.description: Value of the scheme's channel-tag byte for writes to this characteristic (daniao_fragment byte 3): 0 on the command channel; on bulk channels it identifies the buffer type and is chosen per transfer, so a fixed value here only covers the common case.

device.$comment: `category` is required rather than optional because an absent category is not a neutral omission at the consumer: the mobile app has nothing to draw beside the device but a generic radio icon, which is also what it draws for a device whose protocol nobody ever worked out. A spec author always knows what kind of thing they documented, so stating it costs one line and omitting it is paid for by every user of the app.

manufacturer_status.description: Why this device needs open source rescue. Enum kept aligned with the mobile Rust ManufacturerStatus enum (the mobile consumer now supports 'active'). Use 'active' when the manufacturer is still in business and shipping the product but the protocol is closed/proprietary; use 'unsupported' when there is simply no open/official support for third-party interoperability. NOTE: this says what the vendor is doing, not whether the protocol is published -- see `openness`. A device can be 'active' and completely open.

openness.description: Whether this protocol had to be recovered at all. Nearly every spec here documents a closed protocol that somebody worked out from captures, firmware or an app teardown; a few document one whose authors publish it and want third parties to implement it. Those are different kinds of document and should not read alike -- the first is our best reconstruction and can simply be wrong, the second is a summary of somebody else's authoritative text and should send the reader there. Recording which one a spec is also tells a consumer where to look when the protocol changes, and stops the registry implying that everything in it was prised out of a vendor that did not want to be read. Absent means `undocumented`: the default, and by a wide margin the commonest case.

status.description: 'open_by_design': the protocol is published by the people who build the thing and third-party clients are an intended use -- typically open-source firmware or an open standard. Nothing was reverse engineered, and upstream rather than this file is authoritative. 'documented_api': the vendor publishes an official interface, but the product is otherwise closed -- the published surface is often partial, may require an account or a developer agreement, and can be withdrawn. 'undocumented': nothing is published; everything here was recovered by observation. 'hostile': the vendor actively works to stop third-party clients (pinned certificates, signed firmware, client attestation, terms forbidding interoperation) -- documented anyway, but expect it to be broken on purpose.

reverse_engineered.description: True when any part of this spec was recovered by observation rather than read from published documentation. Stated separately from `status` because the two genuinely come apart: a vendor with a documented API usually leaves the interesting half of it undocumented, so a 'documented_api' spec is commonly part citation and part reconstruction. On an 'open_by_design' spec this should be false -- and that is the point of the field, because it says the work here was reading and summarising rather than liberating.

upstream_docs.description: Where the authoritative documentation lives, so a reader can go to the source instead of trusting our summary -- and so a spec that has fallen behind is visibly stale rather than quietly wrong.

covers.description: Which part of this spec the page is the authority for, e.g. 'JSON API state and info objects'. Per-page rather than one blanket link: upstream documentation is rarely uniform in quality, and knowing which sections are cited and which are not is what makes the rest reviewable.

source_code.description: Repository implementing the protocol, where it is public. On an 'open_by_design' device this outranks every other citation: the firmware is the specification, and a constant read straight out of it cannot drift the way prose around it does.

license.description: SPDX identifier of the firmware or reference implementation, where it is public. Worth recording separately from the rest: it decides whether a consumer may fork the device's own software rather than merely speak to it, which is a different and much larger freedom than an open protocol.

testing.description: Whether THIS PROJECT has exercised the spec against real hardware, stated for the spec as a whole. The existing machinery answers narrower questions -- per-fact `verification` grades one claim, `setup.methods[].verified` certifies one onboarding flow, `setup.confidence` grades one section -- and none of them rolls up to the verdict a consumer actually wants first: has anyone driven a device with this document? Absent means nobody has said, which a reader must treat as 'untested'. Reference specs (device.type 'reference-*') document published standards and never carry this block.

status.description: 'untested': no one on this project has driven hardware end-to-end from this spec -- everything here comes from static analysis, published sources, or captures nobody replayed. 'verified': at least one documented flow has been executed against real hardware by this project and behaved as written. The bar for 'verified' is deliberately ours-only: a third-party implementer's success story supports per-fact `verification: reported`, not this flag.

detail.description: Optional refinement of `status`. With status 'untested': 'capture-verified' means key facts were checked against over-the-air captures of real hardware traffic held in our research store -- stronger than static analysis, weaker than driving the device, because a capture shows the vendor app's happy path and nothing else. With status 'verified': 'minimally-verified' means one or a few flows were exercised and the rest of the surface is untouched; 'mostly-verified' means the majority of the documented surface has been driven. A bare status with no detail is the weakest reading of that status.

notes.description: What the claim rests on: which capture files, which hardware unit, which flows were driven, dated. A status without its evidence named is a label a reviewer cannot check.

protocol.description: Primary communication protocol. Enum kept aligned with the mobile Rust Protocol enum. NOTE: 'obd2' covers devices reached through a vehicle diagnostic connector (see the top-level `obd` block); 'uart' and 'can' cover devices on a plain wired local bus with no radio at all (see the top-level `bus` block) -- an e-bike motor talking to its display, for example. The mobile Rust Protocol enum does NOT yet consume any of these three, so such specs are documentation/tooling targets rather than mobile-app targets today; reaching one from a phone needs a bridge.

type.description: Free-form device class, e.g. 'smart-scale' or 'ebike-controller'. One value is load-bearing: a `type` starting with 'reference-' (e.g. 'reference-diagnostic-protocol', 'reference-transport-protocol') marks the file as a published-protocol reference rather than a device. Reference specs document a standard other specs cite instead of restating -- SAE J1979 PIDs, ISO 14229 UDS services, ISO 15765-2 framing -- and so are exempt from the rule that a spec must document an access surface (`services`, `http_endpoints`, `mqtt_topics`, `obd`, `bus` or `cloud`). Say what the thing IS here in whatever words fit; say what KIND of thing it is in `category`, which is the closed vocabulary consumers can actually branch on.

category.description: Broad device class from a CLOSED vocabulary, unlike free-form `type`. This is the field a consumer branches on: the mobile app picks the icon it draws beside a scan result from this value, so a device whose category is missing or unrecognised shows up as an anonymous Bluetooth address next to devices that announce what they are. That is the whole reason the vocabulary is closed -- 'smart-scale', 'kitchen-scale' and 'body-composition-scale' are three useful `type` values and one `category` ('scale'). Pick the category a person would use to describe the device across the room, not the most precise one: an LED strip controller is a 'light', an LED matrix panel is a 'display', an e-bike mid-drive is a 'motor'. Use 'reference' for published-protocol reference specs (the ones whose `type` starts with 'reference-'); they document a standard, not a device. Use 'other' only when nothing else fits, and treat it as a prompt to propose a new value rather than a resting place. Values not in this list are rejected on purpose: a typo'd or invented category is indistinguishable from an unknown one at the consumer, and silently degrades to the generic icon.

pictogram.description: Optional finer-grained visual identity than `category`, for devices worth recognising on sight even when this app does not control them (a MacBook, a Framework laptop, a NAS, a Nintendo console, a UniFi access point, a MikroTik router). A consumer resolves this token to a specific glyph and FALLS BACK to the `category` icon when it does not recognise the token -- so an unknown pictogram never loses the device, exactly as an unknown `category` degrades to the generic icon. Tokens are kebab-case and describe the thing a person sees across the room: e.g. `wifi-ap`, `network-switch`, `router`, `ip-camera`, `video-doorbell`, `nvr`, `nas`, `cloud-key`, `game-console`, `laptop`, `laptop-apple`, `desktop`, `mini-pc`, `smart-speaker`, `3d-printer`, `smoke-alarm`, `thermostat`, `power-station`, `air-quality`, `co2-sensor`, `streaming-stick`, `garage-door`, `label-printer`. The vocabulary is open on purpose; the consumer's resolver owns the token->glyph table and its fallbacks.

admin_url.description: URL template for the device's OWN administration interface, so a consumer can deep-link the user straight to it. Use `{address}` as the placeholder the consumer substitutes with the discovered IP/host (e.g. `https://{address}/`, `http://{address}/webfig/`). This is where a device we only IDENTIFY (see `integration`) sends the user to actually manage it -- a UniFi switch's web UI, a MikroTik router's WebFig. Not a research reference (those go in `helpful_urls`); this is a live control-plane link on the local network.

integration.description: What THIS project's consumers actually DO with the device, as distinct from whether local control is theoretically possible (that is `local_access`). 'supported' (the default when omitted): the app implements a control and/or monitoring surface for it -- the normal case, implied by the presence of services/commands/http_endpoints/camera. 'identify_only': the app deliberately does not speak the device's control protocol; it discovers it, shows a pictogram, and links to its `admin_url`. Network infrastructure (routers, switches, access points) is the archetype -- fully controllable in principle (RouterOS/UniFi APIs) but out of scope here, so we recognise it and hand the user off to its own admin page rather than pretend to manage it. A device can be `identify_only` and still carry a rich `discovery` block: knowing what it is and where it lives is the whole point.

security_advisory.description: A KNOWN, PUBLIC security problem with this device -- a shared/hardcoded key, a replayable command, or a device that should not be trusted at all (a Bluetooth card skimmer). A consumer surfaces this as a WARNING ahead of any control surface: the app badges the scan result, opens a warning page instead of the controls, and for `severity: malicious` raises an alert on sight. Use ONLY for cited, real advisories -- link the writeup in `advisory_url` -- never speculation. This is orthogonal to `openness`/`manufacturer_status` (which describe the vendor and protocol), and to whether the device is otherwise controllable.

severity.description: 'vulnerable': a confirmed, practical exploit exists (e.g. a shared BLE key that unlocks every unit). 'reported': a weaker or unconfirmed problem -- harder to pull off (needs live intercept/replay), or disclosed but unacknowledged by the vendor. 'malicious': the device itself is the threat, not a flawed product -- a card skimmer's Bluetooth module -- and a consumer should alert, not offer control.

summary.description: One line, shown on the scan badge and at the top of the warning. State the risk plainly: 'Shared Bluetooth key lets a nearby attacker unlock and immobilize the car.'

detail.description: The fuller explanation for the warning page: what the flaw is, what an attacker can do, who is affected.

advisory_url.description: The public writeup this is based on -- a research page, a news story, a CVE. Required in spirit: a security_advisory with no citation is speculation.

mitigation.description: How the owner can fix it, when the vendor shipped a patch. Absent means no known fix yet -- which the consumer says explicitly rather than implying safety.

summary.description: One line: what the owner does -- 'Update the firmware in the KARR app'.

url.description: Where to do it, when there is a link (the vendor's patch page or app).

identification.description: How to identify this device during scanning. This is the canonical machine-readable summary of the signals a scanner can see BEFORE connecting: local name, advertised service UUIDs, manufacturer-data company ID and MAC OUI. `device.discovery` carries the full evidence and the payload-level matching rules; anything here should also be derivable from there. Kept separate because a scanner needs a cheap answer to "is this thing worth showing the user?" on every advertisement, and the signals differ sharply in strength -- see `mac_prefixes`.

local_name_prefix.description: BLE advertisement local name prefix. Use `local_name_prefixes` instead when the family ships under several names.

local_name_prefixes.description: Every BLE local name prefix this device family advertises under, for families sold as several rebadged models with no shared prefix (inkbird-bbq-thermometer ships under eight). A match on any one of them means exactly what a `local_name_prefix` match means -- these are alternatives, not a conjunction. May be used together with `local_name_prefix`, in which case a consumer treats the union.

local_names.description: EXACT advertised names matched whole-string, not by prefix. For when a bare factory-default name is the signal and a configured one is not -- a bluetooth card skimmer leaves its module named exactly `HC-05`, where a hobby project renames it. Distinct from `local_name_prefixes`, which matches any name that STARTS with the value.

service_uuids.description: BLE service UUIDs advertised by the device.

manufacturer_data.description: BLE manufacturer-specific advertisement data (AD type 0xFF). Recorded here so a scanner can recognise a device that advertises no usable local name and no service UUID -- common on sensors that broadcast their readings and never expect a connection. Payload layout, byte offsets and prefix patterns belong in `device.discovery`; this block only carries the identifying company ID(s) plus whatever free-form description helps a reader.

company_id.description: Bluetooth SIG company identifier in the manufacturer-data header, as a decimal integer (e.g. 961 for Ember). Note that vendors frequently squat on an ID they do not own -- shining-glasses advertises 21076 because 0x5254 spells 'TR' little-endian -- so a company ID says 'this advertisement looks like the one we documented', not 'this is that vendor'.

company_id_hex.description: The same value written in hex, e.g. '0x03C1'. Redundant with `company_id` and purely for readers -- sources almost always quote the hex form. When both are present they must agree.

description.description: Free-form note on how the ID was established and which firmware uses which -- e.g. whether the value is a real SIG assignment or a squatted one. The analogous `discovery.methods[].ble.manufacturer_data` block declares the same key.

additional_company_ids.description: Further company IDs the same device family advertises, e.g. older firmware or a rebadged model. Govee's H5075 uses 0xEC88 while the H5177 uses 0x0001; SwitchBot moved from 0x0059 to 0x0969. A scanner should treat every ID here as equivalent to `company_id`.

mac_prefixes.description: IEEE OUI prefixes seen on this device's BLE/WiFi MAC address, most-significant octet first, e.g. 'C4:7C:8D'. THIS IS THE WEAKEST IDENTIFYING SIGNAL IN THE BLOCK and must never be used alone to claim a device is supported: an OUI is assigned to a vendor, not a product, so C4:7C:8D matches every Xiaomi radio ever built and not just the plant monitor. Its value is ranking -- an unnamed device with a known vendor OUI is worth showing a user above an unnamed device with an unknown one. Note also that it is unavailable on Apple platforms, where CoreBluetooth hands out a per-host UUID instead of the hardware address, and that BLE privacy-mode devices advertise a random address with no OUI at all. Record only prefixes actually observed or documented by a cited source; do not fill these in from an OUI lookup of the vendor name. Prefixes need not stop on an octet boundary: IEEE also assigns 28-bit MA-M ('C4:7C:8D:6') and 36-bit MA-S ('C4:7C:8D:6A:1') blocks, and a longer prefix is what lets a device inside a subdivided range name its actual vendor instead of the fifteen unrelated ones sharing the octet.

oneOf.description: A bare prefix, which means `confidence: low` -- the safe reading, and the right one for a prefix nobody has checked.

notes.description: Why the confidence is what it is -- who else is in the block, or how exclusivity was established. A confidence with no reasoning behind it is a guess wearing a label.

ssdp_search_targets.description: SSDP/UPnP search targets this device answers to, e.g. `urn:Belkin:device:controllee:1`. The only way to find hardware with no meaningful mDNS presence. Declare vendor-specific targets only: generic UPnP boilerplate like `upnp:rootdevice` is answered by every router, printer and NAS on the link, so a consumer must treat it as a ranking hint rather than an identification -- the same caveat `mac_prefixes` carries.

mdns_service_type.description: mDNS/Bonjour service type for WiFi discovery (e.g. _http._tcp).

lan_protocols.description: Vendor LAN protocols this device identifies itself by *answering*, for hardware that neither advertises mDNS/Bonjour nor responds to SSDP -- the TP-Link Kasa smart-home protocol (`tplink-smarthome`), where a device is found by a UDP broadcast it answers with its full sysinfo. Unlike the passive `mdns_service_type`/`ssdp_search_targets` (which a device volunteers) and unlike `default_port` (which says nothing about who is listening), a positive answer to a vendor protocol probe is a strong identification: only a device that speaks the protocol replies at all. Name the protocol, not the port; a consumer that has completed the handshake tags the device with the same token, and the two are matched. Vendor-specific values only, for the same reason `ssdp_search_targets` must be.

ssid_prefix.description: WiFi SSID prefix when device is in AP mode.

default_port.description: Default TCP port for the device's local API.

discovery.description: How to automatically discover this device on a network. A consumer that parses the schema can implement discovery without per-device hardcoding.

methods.description: Ordered discovery methods to try, first is preferred.

local_name.description: Match the advertised BLE local name. With `match: regex`, `value` is a regular expression tested against the full name (use anchors ^...$ to require a full match). local_name and service_uuids are an EITHER/OR within a ble_scan method: a device matches if its name matches OR it advertises one of the service_uuids — a consumer ORs whichever of the two are present. Give both when a family spans models that are cleanest to catch one way or the other.

service_uuids.description: Advertised GATT service UUIDs to match. OR-combined with local_name (see local_name.description): a scan result matches the method if it satisfies either.

url.description: SSDP response header for the URL. Default LOCATION.

key.description: Short name for this key (udn, serial, mac)

parse_rules.description: How to parse the fetched description: namespace handling, which elements are standard, and what to do with vendor extensions.

example.description: A literal description document, real enough to parse in a test.

port_fallback.description: Ordered port probe list for devices with unstable ports (e.g., Wemo).

request.description: The M-SEARCH datagram itself. A client cannot guess CRLF line endings, the quoted MAN value or the trailing blank line, and SSDP responders reject requests that get them wrong.

mx.description: MX header value: the maximum seconds a device may wait before replying.

example.description: A literal datagram, so an implementation can be diffed against it.

response.description: How to read the unicast replies.

dedupe_by.description: Header a client should deduplicate on — one device answers once per search target.

match.description: How to tell this device's responses from every other UPnP responder on the LAN. Essential whenever ssdp:all is among the search targets, since without it a discovery client reports printers and routers as devices.

timing.description: Listen windows and probe timeouts. The response wait must be at least MX.

udp_broadcast.description: Discovery by a UDP datagram exchange on the local segment: send a probe to a broadcast address (or just listen for the periodic unsolicited beacons many of these protocols emit). Covers Ubiquiti device discovery (port 10001), MikroTik MNDP (5678), TP-Link Kasa (9999), LIFX (56700) and similar. The reply is usually a TLV blob whose fields carry the device's model, name and firmware.

port.description: UDP port the probe is sent to and replies arrive on (Ubiquiti 10001, MNDP 5678, Kasa 9999, LIFX 56700).

broadcast_address.description: Destination for the probe; the directed subnet broadcast (e.g. 10.69.255.255) also works and crosses fewer boundaries.

probe_hex.description: The probe datagram as hex, if the protocol is request/response (Ubiquiti v1 '01000000', MNDP an empty/zero datagram). Omit or leave empty for listen-only protocols that beacon on their own.

passive_ok.description: True when devices broadcast unsolicited beacons, so a consumer can also just listen without probing (MNDP and Ubiquiti both beacon periodically).

response_format.description: Shape of the reply. 'tlv' = type/length/value records (Ubiquiti, MNDP); 'json' = plain JSON; 'json_xor' = JSON under the 0xAB autokey cipher (Kasa); 'json_aes' = JSON under AES (Tuya's 6667 beacon is AES-128-ECB under a fixed, published discovery key); 'binary' = a packed struct (LIFX).

passive_l2.description: Receive-only Layer-2 neighbour discovery: the consumer listens for the periodic multicast frames switches, routers and APs emit, and reads the device's identity out of them. Not routable and not a probe -- it needs a raw/link-layer capture on the local link, and it only sees directly-attached neighbours. LLDP is the vendor-neutral standard; CDP is Cisco's (Ubiquiti and MikroTik can emit LLDP).

protocol.description: 'lldp' (IEEE 802.1AB): EtherType 0x88CC, multicast 01:80:C2:00:00:0E, TLVs (Chassis ID, Port ID, TTL, System Name/Description, Capabilities, Management Address). 'cdp' (Cisco): SNAP multicast 01:00:0C:CC:CC:CC, TLVs (Device-ID, Port-ID, Capabilities, Software version, Platform).

identity.description: How to name and order discovered devices. Stable keys are for collision-resistant identity; display is for user-facing UI.

stable_keys.description: Field names in priority order for stable device identity. First non-empty value wins. BLE typically: ['address']. Wemo: ['udn', 'serial', 'mac']. Vector: ['serial', 'hostname']. 'address' is only a stable key for a device whose BLE address is PUBLIC: a random-static or resolvable-private address rotates, and keying on one makes a client either lose the device it already knows or enrol the same lock twice under two names. When a spec's evidence shows a rotating address, key on something the device carries across the rotation -- a serial-bearing local name, a manufacturer-data payload -- and treat the address as an ephemeral connection locator to be re-resolved by scanning, not as identity.

display.description: Field name for user-facing display. 'friendlyName' for Wemo, 'name' for mDNS, 'local_name' for BLE.

notes.description: Caveats about this identity that the key list alone cannot carry: which keys are only present in some device mode, what a client should do when the top-priority key is missing, or why an obvious-looking key (a rotating BLE address, a DHCP-assigned IP) was deliberately left out.

static_ip_required.description: If true, no automatic network discovery is possible and the user must enter an IP.

setup.description: Initial device setup (provisioning/onboarding): how a factory-fresh — or factory-reset — device is brought onto the user's network and made controllable. This is deliberately distinct from `discovery` (finding an already-provisioned device) and from top-level `initialization` (the per-connection handshake). WiFi devices usually need a real onboarding flow; most BLE devices do not, and should say so with `required: false`.

required.description: Whether the device must be provisioned before it can be discovered and controlled. False for devices that are usable straight out of the box (typical for BLE-only devices).

confidence.description: How well the setup flow is verified. 'high' = confirmed against hardware or a working open implementation; 'medium' = derived from public source/vendor docs but not replayed; 'low' = inferred, needs capture.

methods.description: Ordered onboarding methods to try, first is preferred.

type.description: Onboarding model. 'none' = nothing to provision; 'softap_*' = device hosts a temporary AP and takes credentials over HTTP, SOAP, a UDP datagram protocol or MQTT; 'ble_provisioning' = credentials are pushed over a GATT/BLE protocol; 'ble_direct' = BLE device is usable by scanning and connecting, with no credential exchange; 'wps'/'smartconfig' = WiFi-layer provisioning; 'wired' = Ethernet/USB first-run; 'device_ui' = configured on the device's own screen/controls; 'hub_pairing' = joined to a bridge/hub rather than to WiFi; 'button_pairing' = physical link button authorizes a client; 'cloud_account' = onboarding only exists inside the vendor cloud/app.

softap.description: Details of the temporary access point the device hosts while in setup mode.

ssid_prefix.description: Case-insensitive SSID prefix that identifies the setup AP.

open_network.description: True when the setup AP has no passphrase.

passphrase_source.description: Where the setup AP passphrase comes from when the AP is not open (e.g. 'printed on device sticker').

gateway_ip.description: IP the device answers on while hosting the setup AP.

port.description: Port of the setup API on the setup AP. The transport follows the method type: TCP for softap_http/softap_soap/softap_mqtt, UDP for softap_udp.

credential_encryption.description: How the WiFi passphrase is protected on the wire during provisioning.

padding.description: Block cipher padding scheme, e.g. pkcs7.

key_derivation.description: Where the key material comes from (e.g. 'device metadata returned by GetMetaInfo').

algorithm_steps.description: The encryption as an ordered, unambiguous procedure. Prose like 'AES-128-CBC with a key derived from device metadata' is not implementable; state the byte-level detail — whether values are UTF-8 or hex-decoded, how many hash rounds, the padding, the output encoding.

variants.description: Alternative key derivations where firmware generations differ. Each entry must say how a client decides it applies.

keydata.description: Key material layout for this variant.

selector.description: How a client decides this variant applies.

openssl_equivalent.description: An equivalent openssl(1) invocation, for implementations without a crypto library — and as a second description of the algorithm that can be checked against the first.

test_vectors.description: Known-good values so an implementation can be verified without hardware — the highest-value thing this block can carry. Use a documentation-range MAC and an invented serial so the vectors identify no real device, and add a test asserting they stay reproducible.

input.description: The inputs every vector is derived from.

encoding.description: How the ciphertext is encoded before transmission (e.g. base64 plus hex length suffix).

ble.description: Details of a BLE-based provisioning channel.

advertised_name.description: Name pattern advertised while in setup/pairing mode.

protocol.description: Name of the provisioning protocol (e.g. 'Anki RTS').

pairing_required.description: Whether BLE bonding / a PIN is required before provisioning messages are accepted.

pin_source.description: Where the pairing PIN comes from (device screen, sticker, fixed default).

cloud.description: Details of a cloud-account-only onboarding path.

local_alternative.description: Any known way to provision without the vendor cloud, or an explicit statement that none is known.

verified.description: True only when this exact flow has been executed successfully against hardware. Always state it: an absent flag reads as an oversight rather than as 'not yet verified'.

timing.description: Timing constants a client must honour. Onboarding flows are full of values that look arbitrary but are not (minimum poll timeouts, deliberate duplicate sends); record them rather than leaving the next implementer to rediscover them by failing.

troubleshooting.description: Known failure modes and their causes. Onboarding fails for a small number of recurring reasons — wrong band, unsupported security mode, wrong credential variant — and naming them is often the difference between a working implementation and an abandoned one.

factory_reset.description: How to return the device to its unprovisioned state. Required knowledge for rebinding a device to a new network or a new owner.

applicable.description: Set false when the device has no meaningful factory reset — a vehicle reached over a diagnostic connector, or hardware with no stored state to clear. Set 'unknown' when the device probably has one but nobody has established it; that requires `confidence: low` and no `procedures`. State why in `effect` and omit `procedures` in both cases; inventing a procedure to fill the field is worse than saying there is none, and on safety-relevant hardware it is actively dangerous.

effect.description: What a reset actually clears (credentials, name, rules, pairings, telemetry history).

name.description: Short label, e.g. 'Restore button while powering on'.

applies_to.description: Variant models this procedure applies to; omit when it applies to all.

indicator.description: LED/screen/audio signal that confirms the reset took.

rejoin.description: Moving an already-provisioned device to a different WiFi network or controller (new router, new SSID, new owner).

requires_factory_reset.description: True when there is no in-place way to hand the device new credentials and a reset is the only path.

in_place_supported.description: True when the device accepts new credentials while still joined to the old network (or while reachable by the client).

credentials.description: What secrets the setup flow moves around, so consumers can handle them correctly and users can judge the risk.

wifi_passphrase_protection.description: How the user's WiFi passphrase is protected in transit during provisioning.

stored_on_device.description: Secrets persisted on the device by setup (WiFi passphrase, cloud tokens, pairing keys).

issued_to_client.description: Secrets the device or cloud hands back to the client and that must be stored for later control (API username, bearer GUID, pinned certificate).

variants.description: Distinct device models covered by this one spec because they speak the same protocol, but which differ in command set or in what hardware they actually have -- BLE families sharing service UUIDs, and LAN families sharing a control protocol (the metering and non-metering Kasa plugs answer the same port-9999 JSON). Consumers match a connected device to a variant via its identification block, and an `entities[].variants` list says which models actually expose a given entity: without that pairing a spec draws a permanently unavailable control on the half of the family whose hardware does not have the sensor.

model.description: Model identifier (e.g. 'SP107E'). This string is the name `entities[].variants` refers to, so spell it identically in both places.

identification.description: How to identify this specific variant during scanning.

local_name_prefix.description: BLE advertisement local name prefix that distinguishes this variant.

service_uuids.description: BLE service UUIDs advertised by this variant.

model_prefix.description: Prefix of the model string the device reports about ITSELF, for a LAN device that advertises no BLE local name: TP-Link's get_sysinfo answers `model: "HS110(US)"`, so the prefix 'HS110' matches every region's units. Matched as a prefix precisely because vendors suffix region and hardware-revision codes onto an otherwise stable model name. Where the device also reports a capability list, prefer that at runtime -- a variant table has to be edited when a new model ships, a capability flag does not.

helpful_urls.description: Human-oriented references for this device: teardowns, protocol write-ups, vendor documentation, forum threads and working open implementations. This is not a proof chain for every field; it is the short list that helps the next person understand or reproduce the work without spelunking through notes.

helpful_videos.description: Human-oriented video references for this device: teardown footage, setup walkthroughs, capture demonstrations or protocol explainers. Do not restrict this to YouTube; PeerTube, Vimeo, Invidious and direct video URLs are just as valid when they resolve and are relevant.

references.description: RESERVED, and always invalid. Reference links go in `helpful_urls`; video links go in `helpful_videos`.
references.$comment: Alias trap, and the one place this schema closes a door on purpose. Unknown top-level keys are allowed everywhere else so bespoke per-device blocks can travel alongside the standard fields, and a consumer ignoring a key it does not know is the intended outcome. `references` is the exception because it is not a bespoke block, it is a misspelling of a field that already exists: eighteen specs collected their teardowns, protocol write-ups and working implementations under `references:` and every consumer dropped the lot -- the index generator reads `helpful_urls`, so the links were in the file, out of the artifact, and nothing anywhere said so. Permissiveness cannot distinguish 'a key we do not understand' from 'a key we do understand, spelled wrong'; naming the wrong spelling is what makes the difference legible. Scoped to the top level deliberately: a `references:` nested inside a bespoke block (devolo's `zwave:` cites OpenZWave and openHAB database entries there) is prose citation, not a link list, and stays legal.

not.$comment: the key `references` is not read by anything -- rename it to `helpful_urls` (or `helpful_videos` for video links) and give each entry a `title` and a `url`

protocol_handler.description: Names a consumer-side (e.g. Rust) handler implementation to dispatch to for devices whose protocol cannot be fully expressed in YAML (image assembly, custom crypto, etc.). Lets a registry select the right code path automatically instead of hardcoding a device->handler map.

features.description: Declares high-level device capabilities that go beyond raw GATT reads/writes. The capability is declarative; some (e.g. image_upload) require dedicated consumer-side code to implement.

type.description: Capability type. `stored_upload` persists content ON the device so it plays standalone after disconnect (distinct from `image_upload`, which streams live frames).

container_format.description: Names the consumer-side encoder that builds the persisted file blob for a `stored_upload` (e.g. `daniao_amx`). Like `protocol_handler` for the live path: the container layout (protobuf + CRC over a base template) cannot be declarative, so the spec names an algorithm the consumer implements.

file_type.description: The transport's file-kind tag for a `stored_upload` (Daniao's UploadRequest.type: 3 = animation/microapp, 0 = effect .eff).

frame_size.description: Payload bytes per data packet for a `stored_upload`'s transport, when the device fixes one (Daniao's is 500).

play_command.description: Command (named from a characteristic's `commands`) that plays a stored item by its id right after a `stored_upload` — the vendor's store-then-show. Absent means store without auto-playing.

response_characteristic.description: Characteristic UUID the device answers a `stored_upload` on (Daniao: the DDP Notify characteristic carrying M_UPLOAD_START_RESPONSE mt=2931 and M_UPLOAD_COMPLETE mt=2934). A client should wait for the completion message before sending `play_command` — the vendor app does, and playing a cid the device has not committed yet is a silent no-op.

max_width.description: Maximum image width in pixels (for image_upload).

max_height.description: Maximum image height in pixels (for image_upload).

format.description: Binary format the device expects for uploaded assets. `zlib-bmp` is a zlib/DEFLATE-compressed 24-bit Windows BMP, built app-side and carried as the compressed blob (e.g. the LOY SPACE `zip_bmp` field, Base64-inside-JSON) — distinct from a raw `gif`, which the device decodes itself.

resolution_source.description: Whether max_width/max_height are the panel's actual size ('fixed') or platform upper bounds with the real per-model resolution reported by the device at runtime ('device_reported'). Clients should let the user set the canvas size for device_reported panels they have not yet queried.

resolution_advertisement.description: For 'device_reported' panels: where the real width/height sit in the BLE advertisement's manufacturer-specific data, so a client can default the canvas to the true panel size before connecting. Offsets index the manufacturer-data VALUE (bytes after the 2-byte company id).

company_id.description: Bluetooth SIG company id of the manufacturer-data record carrying the resolution.

width_offset.description: Byte offset of width within the manufacturer-data value.

height_offset.description: Byte offset of height within the manufacturer-data value.

animation.description: Whether the device accepts multi-frame sequences (animations), not just a single static image (for image_upload).

channel_tag.description: Value of the framing scheme's channel-tag byte that THIS flow writes under, when the bulk characteristic cannot state one because its tag varies per transfer. SmartDawn's BIN channel carries four buffer types (1=TUTU_DOODLE, 2=TUTU_ERASE, 4=TUTU_RESTORE, 16=MUSIC_BIN) and an image upload is a full-canvas redraw, so this flow is 4. Read together with the characteristic's `framing.channel_tag`, which states a tag fixed for the channel itself.

session_open.description: Commands a client must send, IN THIS ORDER, before the first frame of an upload — named from this spec's own `commands`, so their bytes stay in the command templates and only the choreography lives here. SmartDawn's is `[ui_end_sync, doodle_start]`: the first suspends UI-mirror playback, the second opens the doodle session, and sending the wrong opener (M_DEV_START) blanks the canvas instead. Send once per upload, not once per frame. An EMPTY array states that this device takes pixel data with no preamble at all — which is a different claim from omitting the key, and the distinction is load-bearing: a consumer that implemented a device's flow before this key existed falls back to whatever opener it hardcoded when the key is absent, and would otherwise send that opener to a device that wants none. State it explicitly rather than leaving it to be inferred.
session_open.$comment: This is the one part of an upload flow a handler cannot derive: which commands and in what order is device-specific knowledge, where fragmentation and chunk sizing are properties the framing block already states. Without it a consumer has to hardcode the names, and a device whose opener differs needs a code change rather than a spec change.

max_frames.description: Maximum frames per uploaded animation, when the device stores sequences and the limit is known.

min_frame_interval_ms.description: Fastest supported frame interval in milliseconds — the lower bound for animation-rate controls.

default_frame_interval_ms.description: Frame interval a client should default its animation-rate control to.

allOf.$comment: A service with no characteristics is only worth listing if it says why none are documented. Without that, a reader cannot tell 'this service is empty' from 'nobody has dumped it yet', and the gap invites someone to guess UUIDs -- which is exactly what this repo does not do.

notes.description: Free-form notes about the service. Required when `characteristics` is omitted, where it must say why no characteristic is documented -- e.g. the service is advertised by a variant whose UUIDs were never extracted.

properties.description: BLE characteristic properties. Enum kept aligned with the mobile Rust CharacteristicProperty enum.

allOf.$comment: An advanced opcode must explain itself: consumers are required to surface advanced_reason at the opt-in point, which is impossible if it is absent or empty.

A locate action is offered as a one-tap button with no confirmation -- that is the whole point of it. An advanced command is one a user must not trip into. A command cannot be both, and the combination is exactly the authoring slip worth catching: `flash_firmware` reads as a locator to anything matching on names.

advanced.description: Marks an opcode as advanced: it goes further than a typical consumer app would, because it can damage hardware, void a warranty, alter a vehicle's legal classification, or otherwise carry consequences a casual user would not expect. This is a SIGNPOST, NOT A GATE. Consumers SHOULD keep the capability available and put it behind a deliberate action (a toggle, a confirmation) so nobody trips into it by accident, and SHOULD surface `advanced_reason` at that moment. Consumers SHOULD NOT hide it, require an account for it, or nag: the intended users include repair cafes, independent technicians and owners doing their own maintenance. Absent or false means an ordinary command.
advanced.$comment: Advisory metadata: it does not change how the command is encoded or transmitted. Orthogonal to confidence -- `advanced` says what happens if the command works, not how sure we are that it works.

verification.description: How much weight this command's byte sequence carries. Same vocabulary the OBD blocks use, so confidence is machine-readable rather than buried in prose. Orthogonal to `advanced`: this says how sure we are the command works, `advanced` says what happens when it does.

protocol_id.description: Which of the framing scheme's protocols this command's packet is sent under, when the characteristic declares a `framing.scheme` that carries one (seeblue_envelope byte 3). Part of the envelope, not of the packet: it is why the command's `template` does not contain it.

command_id.description: The command's opcode within its `protocol_id`, where the scheme numbers them. Documentation of the packet's first byte, which the `template` still emits -- stating it separately is what lets a reader match this command against the vendor's own numbering.

ui_id.description: For a UI-change command, the vendor's control identifier the packet addresses.

ui_id_range.description: Inclusive [first, last] `ui_id` bounds for a command that stands for a whole band of controls rather than one, so the id travels as a parameter.

ui_id_min.description: Lower bound of an open-ended `ui_id` band, where the upper end is not known.

setting_id.description: Symbolic setting/enum identifier for a protobuf-style command that names what it sets rather than emitting raw bytes (AdMore's light bar). NOTE: declarative -- a consumer needs a protobuf handler for the device to send one, and the mobile encoder reports such a command as unencodable rather than guessing at bytes.

fixed_length.description: Total bytes on the wire for a command whose frame is a fixed width regardless of payload, so the encoder pads to it. ProGlow's colour packets are always 20 bytes with the unused RGB triples zero-filled.

packet_layout.description: Byte-by-byte description of the frame, keyed by offset. Documentation for a reader checking a capture against the spec, not an encoding instruction -- `template` is what a client executes, and the two must agree.

observed.description: True when this command was seen on the wire during capture, as opposed to being read out of a decompiled app. Narrower than `verification`, which rates the whole byte sequence.

locate.description: Declares this command a locator -- 'make the device noticeable so I can find it' -- and says by which modality: 'sound' for a beep or buzzer, 'flash' for an LED, 'both' when the device does whichever it has. It is the spec-command analogue of the SIG Immediate Alert service (0x1802), for the many devices that implement the same idea with a vendor opcode instead. State it ONLY for a command whose entire effect is to be noticeable and which stops on its own or on user action: not for one that configures an alert (`set_alarm`, `set_flash_count`), reads one back (`get_alarm_mode`), silences one (`silence_alarm`), or changes any persistent setting. Without this key a consumer has nothing to go on but the command's name, and the names in this catalogue do not support that: `play_effect`, `set_mode` and `identify` all read as locators and none is one, while `flash_firmware` reads as one and must never be a tap away. A command marked `advanced` may not carry this key.
locate.$comment: Advisory metadata: it does not change how the command is encoded. Sensible on a fixed `value` command; a consumer offering one-tap locate has no user to supply parameters, so a templated command carrying `locate` is only usable if every parameter has a default.

advanced_reason.description: Short human-readable explanation shown to the user at the opt-in point. State what changes, the realistic consequence, and how to recover -- concrete beats scary. Good: 'Raises the motor current limit; above the motor's rating this can overheat the primary gear. Read and save the current block first so you can restore it.' Bad: 'Dangerous - advanced users only.' Do not moralise or tell the user not to proceed; note the consequence once, factually. Required when `advanced` is true.

value.description: Fixed byte sequence for this command.

template.description: Parameterized byte sequence. Strings are parameter references.

encoding.description: How the command payload is serialized. 'bytes' is a raw byte sequence (value/template); 'json' and 'tlv' commands describe their payload via the `payload` object. NOTE: the mobile Rust parser currently assumes 'bytes'; json/tlv require dedicated handler code.

payload.description: Structured payload description for json/tlv encoded commands. A raw byte sequence does NOT go here: a fixed one is `value`, a parameterized one is `template`.
payload.$comment: `additionalProperties: false` here, against the permissive habit of the rest of this schema, because `payload` is the block a byte sequence is most likely to be misfiled into -- `payload: {bytes: [...]}` reads perfectly and is not a field. Two Govee specs wrote exactly that, and what it cost is the argument for closing the list. The mobile Rust crate grew a bespoke shim to read `payload.bytes` back, so the plug kept working there and the misfiling stopped being visible to the one consumer that could have reported it; every other consumer -- the JSON API, the index, anything reading the schema -- saw commands carrying no bytes at all. The bulb was worse: its arrays were 3-to-7-byte prefixes of a 20-byte frame, so the shim faithfully emitted short writes the hardware rejects, and a spec that looked complete drove nothing. An unknown key elsewhere in this schema is bespoke metadata travelling alongside the standard fields, which is the design; an unknown key HERE is a byte sequence that has gone missing, and no consumer can tell the difference without a shim per vendor. The closed list is what makes the mistake fail loudly, once, in CI.

key.description: Payload key/field name (or TLV tag name).

value_type.description: Type of the payload value (e.g. string, int, bool).

parameters.description: Command parameter definitions, keyed by parameter name. Every key is a parameter: there are no reserved siblings. Channel byte order for a colour command is stated by the order the `template` names `{red}`/`{green}`/`{blue}`, which is where the bytes actually come from -- a device wanting GRB is written `template: ["{green}", "{red}", "{blue}"]`. A separate `color_order` key used to live here and was removed: it restated the template with no defined precedence, so a spec whose two statements disagreed had no correct reading.

allOf.$comment: `min`/`max` bound a NUMBER. A `bytes` parameter is a run of octets with no numeric range, so a bound on one can only have meant its length -- which is what `min_length`/`max_length` say. Fardriver wrote `data: {type: bytes, min: 1, max: 26}` meaning 1-26 bytes; a consumer reading it as a value range rejected the parameter and lost the whole spec with it. Left legal, the two readings are indistinguishable and each is plausible.

default.description: Value a client sends when it supplies none itself, in RAW wire terms. This is what lets a high-level control send only the parameter it owns -- a brightness slider fills `{brightness}` and the protocol filler around it (`seq`, `flag`, a mode byte the command implies) comes from here. A parameter with no default and no caller value has nothing to encode, so the write fails rather than guessing.

allowed.description: The complete set of RAW values the device accepts, when it is a set rather than a range. A consumer offers a choice among these instead of a min..max control -- the difference between picking 'Channel 2' and hunting for 0x02 on a 0-255 slider. Use `min`/`max` when every value in between is meaningful.

labels.description: Human-readable names for `allowed`, paired by index. Only meaningful alongside `allowed`, and the two lengths must match exactly: a consumer that finds them mismatched should keep the values and drop the labels rather than pair them off by position and mislabel a control.

notes.description: Per-parameter caveats the structured fields cannot carry.

endianness.description: Byte order this parameter's value is emitted in. Same key, enum and default as a `format` field's and a bus field's -- encode and decode ask one question and must not answer it two ways. Little is the default because it is what BLE overwhelmingly uses; a `big` parameter must say so, because a byte-swapped write is silently plausible rather than visibly broken.

min_length.description: Fewest octets this `bytes` parameter may carry. The length vocabulary for `bytes`, where `min`/`max` are the value vocabulary for numbers -- state a fixed width as equal `min_length`/`max_length` (a two-byte CRC is 2 and 2).

max_length.description: Most octets this `bytes` parameter may carry, in the same terms as `min_length`.

type.description: Parameter value type. `varint` is a protobuf base-128 varint (LEB128, unsigned): variable width, used for protobuf command fields whose value can exceed 127 (e.g. SmartDawn brightness 0-255). int32/uint32/varint are all consumed by the mobile Rust encoder.

description.description: What this parameter means — the sentence that stops the next reader guessing. State the real-world quantity here even when the shared number-semantics fields cannot carry it alone, e.g. a uint16 value split across two uint8 template slots, where each byte parameter should say which half it is.

min.description: Minimum RAW wire value. Stated in raw terms because it bounds the bytes the template emits; the real-world bound is min * scale + value_offset.

max.description: Maximum RAW wire value, in the same raw terms as `min`.

auto.description: Marks a parameter the encoder fills in itself rather than a value the user sets — without this flag a generic command UI renders one control per declared parameter and would happily show a slider for a checksum byte. 'sequence': a per-message counter the encoder increments (SmartDawn `sn`). 'packet_length': the total encoded packet length (SmartDawn `len`). 'checksum': an additive frame checksum — the byte is the sum (mod 256) of all encoded frame bytes from index `checksum_start` up to but not including this parameter's own position, then XOR `checksum_xor`. This covers the common sum8-over-frame idiom (KingSmith WiLink sums from index 1 with no xor; UREVO UR frames sum from index 1 and xor 0x5A) without a per-device handler. 'xor_checksum': the same span reduced with XOR instead of addition — every Govee 20-byte frame ends in one, over bytes 0..18 (`checksum_start: 0`). 'crc16_modbus': CRC-16/MODBUS over the same span — reflected polynomial 0xA001, init 0xFFFF, no final xor — for MODBUS-RTU framing (Bluetti's `[addr][function][payload][crc lo][crc hi]`, `checksum_start: 0` because the address byte is covered). It is TWO bytes, so the parameter declares `type: uint16`, and MODBUS puts the low byte first, which is this schema's default `endianness`. A parameter carrying `auto` SHOULD still declare its wire `type` so the encoder knows how wide the computed value is. A consumer must never present an auto parameter as a control. NOTE: declarative -- a consumer that does not compute these cannot send the command, which is the honest outcome, since inventing the bytes would produce a packet the device rejects.
auto.$comment: 'xor_checksum' and 'crc16_modbus' are separate ENUM VALUES rather than modifier keys (`checksum_op: xor`) beside 'checksum', and the choice is about how an old consumer fails. A modifier key is an unknown key, which every consumer here is built to ignore -- so it would read `auto: checksum`, compute an ADDITIVE sum over a frame that wanted something else, and send bytes the device silently drops, with a spec that validates and a UI that looks like it worked. An unrecognised `auto` VALUE cannot be mistaken for a mode the reader knows: it fails, which is what this key's own NOTE asks for. The cost is that it fails hard -- a strict enum reader (the mobile Rust crate) rejects the whole spec, not just the command -- so a consumer SHOULD treat an `auto` value it does not know as 'this command is unencodable' and keep the rest of the device. Each value names a COMPLETE algorithm rather than composing one from parts (width, polynomial, init, reflect, xorout): a spec that got one part wrong would still validate and still emit a plausible-looking wrong checksum, and CRC parameter soup is famously easy to get wrong. Naming whole algorithms keeps the failure at 'this reader does not implement crc16_modbus', which is checkable.

checksum_start.description: First frame-byte index included in an `auto: checksum` / `auto: xor_checksum` / `auto: crc16_modbus` span. Defaults to 1 because the additive idiom's frame leader (0xF7 on KingSmith WiLink, the UR header on UREVO) is almost always excluded — it is a framing marker, not payload, and protocols that sum it in are the exception. Govee's XOR frames and MODBUS-RTU are both exceptions and say `checksum_start: 0` (MODBUS covers the address byte). Only meaningful alongside an `auto` checksum role.

checksum_xor.description: Value XORed into an `auto: checksum` result after the mod-256 sum (e.g. 0x5A on UREVO UR frames). Present because a fixed xor constant is how vendors salt an otherwise trivially guessable sum8; absent means 0 (plain additive checksum, as on KingSmith WiLink). Only meaningful alongside `auto: checksum` — it is a salt on the additive result, NOT the reduction operator, which is why an XOR-reduced frame is `auto: xor_checksum` and not this key.

type.description: Field value type. int32/uint32 are consumed by the mobile Rust ValueType enum (4-byte fixed width, endianness honored) — do not work around them with prose or paired uint16 fields.

endianness.description: Byte order of a multi-byte integer field. Same key, same enum and same default as a bus message field's `endianness` — a BLE characteristic and a CAN frame have the same question to answer, and answering it two ways would be a trap. Little-endian is the default because it is what BLE characteristics overwhelmingly use (the SIG's own profiles are little-endian throughout), so the specs that state it are confirming rather than overriding. A `big` field must say so: a byte-swapped decode is silently plausible — a big-endian 0x0100 reads as 1 rather than 256 — so nothing downstream can catch the mistake.

notes.description: Per-field caveats that the structured fields cannot carry — a display rounding the app applies on top of the linear decode, an inferred rather than confirmed unit, a valid subrange.

format.description: Binary format of readable/notifiable characteristic values. Each field may also carry the shared number-semantics vocabulary — `unit`, `scale`, `value_offset`, `unit_source`/`unit_reference`/`unit_values`, `values` — saying what the number means (see $defs/number_semantics).

http_endpoints.description: HTTP/REST API endpoints for WiFi devices.

service.description: Service the action belongs to, as the device names it — for SOAP/UPnP a serviceType URN like 'urn:Belkin:service:basicevent:1'. The machine-readable form of what `description` was already stating in prose, and the key a client resolves the real control URL by from the device's own service list (published paths move across firmware generations, so `path` here is convention, not address). State it on every endpoint an entity's `state_command` names: without it, a consumer that must build a SOAPACTION header for a state read has nowhere to get the URN but prose.

status.description: Whether the endpoint can be built against. 'sunset' records one the vendor removed (Roku dropped /search/browse in OS 12.0): kept for older firmware, but a consumer must not offer a control on it. 'unverified' records one whose existence rests on a probe or a capture rather than documentation or replay (SmartThings' port-8081 root). Absent means active and usable.

unit.description: Unit of this field's value ('C', '%', 'seconds'). JSON payloads carry decoded numbers, so there is no scale to declare — but C-vs-F still needs stating, and `min`/`max` here are read in this unit.

example.description: A literal request body, as bytes go out. Worth its space wherever the envelope is not obvious from the field list — a SOAP action, a form encoding, anything where the field names alone do not say where they sit in the document. It is what an implementer diffs against when the device rejects a request that looks right.

unit.description: Unit of this field's value ('C', '%', 'seconds'). JSON payloads carry decoded numbers, so unlike BLE/bus fields there is no scale to declare — but C-vs-F and W-vs-mW still need stating.

example.description: A literal response body. The one an implementer parses first, so it must be real enough to test against: an entity bound to this endpoint should be derivable from it and nothing else. Same role as `payload_formats.<name>.example`, one level up — that one is a value, this is the document carrying it.

mqtt_topics.description: MQTT topics for cloud-connected or local-broker WiFi devices.

topic.description: MQTT topic pattern. May contain {device_id} or similar placeholders.

direction.description: Message direction from the app's perspective.

unit.description: Unit of this field's value ('C', '%', 'seconds'). JSON payloads carry decoded numbers, so unlike BLE/bus fields there is no scale to declare — but C-vs-F and W-vs-mW still need stating.

camera.description: How to obtain a live video (or single-frame) feed from a device that has a camera, so a consumer can render it locally. Separate from `services`/`http_endpoints` because a feed is a media transport (RTSP, MJPEG, HLS, WebRTC), not a control call, and often lives on a DIFFERENT host than the camera itself (a UniFi Protect camera streams from its NVR, not from the camera). A device with this block is normally `integration: supported` -- exposing the feed is the support.

streams.description: One entry per selectable feed (quality tier, or a distinct transport).

transport.description: 'rtsp'/'rtsps' = RTSP(S) video; 'mjpeg' = multipart MJPEG stream; 'mjpeg_snapshot_poll' = poll a single JPEG at target_fps (the Snapmaker U1 stock camera works this way); 'hls'/'webrtc' as named.

url_template.description: Feed URL with placeholders the consumer substitutes. Use {address} for the feed host (which may be `feed_host_source`, not the device's own IP), {stream_id} for a per-stream token resolved via `stream_discovery`, and {port} where variable. E.g. rtsp://{address}:7447/{stream_id} , http://{address}/server/files/camera/monitor.jpg

default_port.description: Default transport port (RTSP 7447, RTSPS 7441 for UniFi Protect).

served_by.description: Which host serves the feed. 'nvr': an aggregator on the LAN (UniFi Protect NVR) — combine `url_template` with the NVR address, not the camera's.

target_fps.description: For mjpeg_snapshot_poll: how often to fetch the JPEG (the U1 writes ~1 fps).

auth.description: How the feed is authorized: 'none' (RTSP token IS the secret), 'session_cookie', 'basic', etc.

feed_host_source.description: Where the feed host comes from when it is not the device itself: e.g. 'nvr' (a UniFi Protect NVR discovered separately), 'device' (the camera's own IP). Substituted into {address} in the stream url_template.

stream_discovery.description: How to obtain the per-stream token/id and confirm the stream is enabled, when url_template needs a {stream_id}.

method.description: e.g. 'unifi_protect_bootstrap': GET /proxy/protect/api/bootstrap after local login, read cameras[].channels[].rtspAlias where isRtspEnabled is true.

enabled_flag.description: The field that says the stream is on, e.g. 'cameras[].channels[].isRtspEnabled'.

keepalive.description: Some cameras only produce frames while a monitor session is held open. Describe the call to start/maintain it (the Snapmaker U1 needs camera.start_monitor over WebSocket, re-sent every ~5-10 s, before its monitor.jpg refreshes).

start.description: The call that starts the feed, e.g. 'JSON-RPC camera.start_monitor over ws://{address}/websocket, params {domain:lan, interval:0}'.

interval_seconds.description: Re-send the start call at least this often to keep frames flowing.

stop.description: The call that stops it, e.g. 'camera.stop_monitor'.

enable_required.description: True when the feed is OFF by default and a human must turn it on out-of-band before any of this works — UniFi Protect RTSP is disabled per-camera per-quality until enabled in the Protect UI.

enable_notes.description: How to enable the feed when enable_required is true.

obd.description: Diagnostic access for devices reached through a vehicle diagnostic connector (OBD-II / UDS) rather than a radio.
