Vehicles are safety-critical: entries here describe read paths and owner-facing maintenance functions only, and any request whose `verification` is not 'confirmed' must be treated as untested.

role.description: What this device IS on the diagnostic link, which is the first thing that distinguishes OBD-II specs from each other. 'vehicle' = the thing being diagnosed (a bike, a car). 'adapter' = the dongle that bridges a host to the connector; its `adapter_profile` says what it can do. 'module' = a single ECU or accessory documented on its own rather than as part of a whole vehicle. 'reference' = no physical device at all: a published protocol table (SAE J1979 PIDs, ISO 14229 UDS services) that other specs cite instead of restating; pair it with a `device.type` starting with 'reference-'.

adapter_profile.description: Capability classification, meaningful when `role` is 'adapter'. The class is the headline; `capabilities` is what a consumer should actually match request requirements against.

class.description: Capability tier. 'basic-clone': cloned ELM327 firmware — legislated single-frame reads only, unreliable beyond. 'standards-elm327': genuine ELM327 v1.4/1.5 behaviour. 'advanced-stn': STN chipset (OBDLink LX/MX+/CX) — reliable multi-frame transmit, client flow control, ST extensions. 'native-can': a real CAN interface (SocketCAN, PCAN, Kvaser) with no AT-command layer between the client and the bus.

capabilities.description: Everything this adapter class can be relied on to do.

known_limitations.description: Behaviour that fails or is unreliable on this class, in plain language.

connector.description: Physical diagnostic socket on the vehicle.

standard.description: Connector standard: 16-pin automotive (sae-j1962), 6-pin Euro 5 motorcycle (iso-19689), or vendor-specific.

location.description: Where the socket is on the vehicle, e.g. 'under the pillion seat'.

model_years.description: Which model years use this connector, when a vehicle changed connectors mid-life.

pins.description: Pin assignments that matter for diagnostics.

transport.description: Link and transport layer used to reach the ECU.

standard.description: Diagnostic link standard. 'iso15765-4' is CAN with ISO-TP segmentation.

bitrate.description: Bus bitrate in bit/s (500000 for the usual OBD-II CAN variant).

functional_id.description: Functional broadcast request ID (0x7DF on standard OBD-II).

tester_present_ms.description: Interval at which TesterPresent (3E 00) must be sent to hold a non-default session.

description_files.description: Vehicle-level ECU-description files — typically the .grp group files that dispatch to per-variant .prg SGBDs.

adapter_requirements.description: Adapter constraints observed in practice, e.g. functions that only work with an STN-chipset adapter because they need multi-frame ISO-TP with custom headers.

ecus.description: Nodes on the diagnostic bus and which data each owns. Knowing the owner matters when a value displayed on one module is stored in another.

owns.description: Data this node is believed to store, e.g. 'odometer', 'service interval'.

description_files.description: ECU-description files covering this module — the .prg SGBD and the .grp that selects it.

requests.description: Diagnostic requests, including hypotheses that have not been captured yet. Every entry carries its own `verification` so unproven candidates can be recorded without being mistaken for facts.

command_class.description: The dividing line that decides which adapters can run this request. 'basic': legislated OBD-II (SAE J1979 modes), single-frame, no session or security prerequisite — works on essentially any adapter including clones. 'advanced': manufacturer or UDS territory — needs a non-default session, security access, custom headers, or multi-frame ISO-TP, and therefore a capable adapter. Defaults to 'advanced' so an unclassified request is never assumed to be the safe kind.

requires.description: Adapter capabilities this request depends on. Match against `adapter_profile.capabilities` to know before connecting whether a given dongle can run it.

service.description: UDS/OBD service byte in hex, e.g. '22' (ReadDataByIdentifier), '31' (RoutineControl).

prerequisites.description: Ordered requests that must succeed first (session control, security access).

security_access_required.description: Whether a SecurityAccess (27) seed/key exchange is needed before this request is accepted.

writes.description: True if this request mutates vehicle state. Consumers should gate these behind explicit confirmation.

job.description: Name of the job in the referenced description file that this request implements, e.g. an EDIABAS SGBD job name. Ties a recovered frame back to its authoritative definition.

results.description: Result names the reply carries, as named by the description file (e.g. STAT_SERVICE_KMSTAND_DATA). These are how a consumer looks up scaling and units rather than hardcoding offsets.

advanced.description: True for functions that need expertise to use safely — ECU coding and flashing, immobiliser and key operations, adaptation writes, brake-system procedures. These are IN SCOPE and documented: reviving an old bike routinely needs them. The flag tells a consumer to warn and to require confirmation, not to hide the function. Pair with `notes` describing the specific risk (bricking, a module that must be re-coded to the vehicle, a procedure that continues in the service manual).

data_identifiers.description: Known or suspected ReadDataByIdentifier (22) DIDs and how to decode them.

did.description: Data identifier in hex. Four digits is the ISO 14229 two-byte DID used by ReadDataByIdentifier (0x22), e.g. '0xF190'. Six digits is a three-byte read address, which is what vendor dialects that predate UDS put on the wire -- Subaru SSM addresses such as '0x000008' are three address bytes, so truncating them to two would name a different location.

scale.description: Multiplier applied to the raw value to get `unit`. Use `formula` instead when the conversion has an offset or is otherwise not a single multiply.

formula.description: Decode expression in terms of the raw value `x`, e.g. 'x - 40' or '(x - 128) * 0.78125'. Present because most real scalings carry an offset, which `scale` alone cannot express -- reducing '(x - 128) * 0.78125' to 0.78125 silently drops the offset and yields a wrong reading.

source.description: Where this identifier and its scaling came from, e.g. a vendor ECU definition entry.

extended_parameters.description: Vendor logging parameters whose read address is not a constant: it is defined per-ROM in an ECU definition file and differs between calibrations, so it cannot be written down here. RomRaider's Subaru 'extended' params are the case this exists for. They are identified by the vendor's parameter id and resolved against the matching ECU def at read time -- listing one under `data_identifiers` would mean inventing an address.

logparam.description: Vendor parameter id as the ECU definition names it, e.g. 'E21'.

scale.description: Multiplier applied to the raw value to get `unit`.

formula.description: Decode expression in terms of the raw value `x`.

source.description: Which ECU definition this parameter and its scaling came from.

cloud.description: A vendor cloud service the device depends on. Present ONLY to record the dependency honestly -- this is the problem, not the interface we want consumers to build on. A spec may satisfy the schema with `cloud` alone, which is precisely the 'cloud-only, no local path' case: it makes that state machine-readable instead of leaving it as prose in a notes field, so a consumer can say 'this device stops working when the vendor does' rather than silently offering endpoints that will one day 404. Pair with `local_access` to record what, if anything, would free it.

required.description: True when the device's documented functions do not work without this service. This is the flag that marks a device cloud-only.

vendor_service.description: Human-readable name of the service, e.g. 'NIU cloud'.

hosts.description: Base hosts, e.g. 'https://app-api-fk.niu.com'. Note where hosts are region-dependent.

auth.description: How a client authenticates. Record the shape only -- NEVER a real token, credential, account identifier or device serial.

endpoint.description: Path that issues the credential, e.g. '/v3/api/oauth2/token'.

endpoints.description: Documented cloud endpoints. Recorded as evidence of the dependency and because they are useful while the service lives -- not as a local control surface.

returns.description: What the response carries, in prose.

failure_mode.description: What actually stops working when the service goes away or the account is closed. State it concretely -- this is the sentence a user needs before buying or keeping the device.

data_leaves_device.description: Categories of data the device sends to the vendor, e.g. 'location', 'ride history'. Flag anything that is personal data about a person rather than telemetry about a machine.

local_access.description: Whether this device can be controlled without the vendor's service, and what it takes. Answers the question a repair café asks first: 'can I actually do anything with this one?' Applies to any spec, not only cloud devices.

status.description: 'native': the device speaks a local protocol as shipped -- the normal case in this registry. 'bridge_hardware': a local interface exists but reaching it needs an adapter that is not part of the product (a BLE-to-UART bridge, a CAN interface). 'replacement_hardware': no local interface exists on the stock part, and local control means swapping a component for an aftermarket one. 'firmware_replacement': the stock hardware can be freed, but only by replacing its firmware. 'none_known': no path known today -- an honest dead end, not an omission.

covers.description: Functions the local path actually gives you.

not_covered.description: Functions that REMAIN cloud- or vendor-dependent even after taking this path. Filling this in matters: aftermarket hardware routinely frees one subsystem while leaving the rest tethered, and a spec that omits this reads as a bigger win than it is.

hardware.description: Known hardware that provides or restores local access. Recorded as documentation of what exists, not as an endorsement or a purchase recommendation.

url.description: Product or project page. Third-party commercial listings change and go dead; treat as a pointer, not a citation.

role.description: 'bridge': sits alongside the stock hardware and exposes an existing local interface. 'replacement_part': substitutes a stock component. 'diagnostic_adapter': connects a host to an existing diagnostic or debug interface. 'programmer': writes firmware or parameters.

replaces.description: Stock component this substitutes, when role is replacement_part.

fits.description: Models this is sold as fitting.

reversible.description: Whether the stock part can be refitted afterwards. Worth stating -- it is the difference between an experiment and a commitment.

bus.description: A plain wired local bus -- UART/TTL serial or raw CAN -- for devices with no radio and no diagnostic connector. An e-bike motor talking to its display lives here. Distinct from `obd`: that models a diagnostic session (connector standard, ECU addressing, UDS services, security access) reached through a standardised socket, whereas this models an internal bus whose traffic is simply there to be read. A consumer needs a physical adapter to reach one of these, so specs here are documentation and bridge-building targets. Vehicles: the same care as `obd` applies -- anything that transmits on a bus with a motor on it is `advanced`.

link.description: Physical layer parameters -- what you set on the adapter before any byte makes sense.

type.description: 'uart': asynchronous TTL serial, point-to-point on a harness line. 'can': a CAN bus carrying raw frames (NOT ISO-TP diagnostics -- that is `obd`).

baud.description: UART baud rate, e.g. 1200 (Bafang BBS02) or 9600 (Tongsheng TSDZ2). Getting this wrong yields plausible-looking garbage, so it is worth stating even when it seems obvious.

logic_level.description: Signalling level where it matters for adapter choice, e.g. '3.3V TTL'.

wiring.description: How to physically reach the bus: which wire or pin carries what.

signal.description: Signal on this conductor, e.g. 'CAN-H', 'motor TX', 'ground'.

connector.description: Connector this pin belongs to, e.g. 'D-Sub 9 (CiA DS-102)', '6-pin Tongsheng'.

style.description: How traffic is organised, which decides what a consumer must implement. 'request_response': the host asks and the device answers, so messages carry `request`/`response` (Bafang BBS02). 'stream': both ends push fixed-shape packets at a fixed rate with nobody asking, so messages carry `start_byte` and `rate_hz` -- and note that transmitting at all means continuously asserting state (Tongsheng TSDZ2). 'broadcast': nodes emit frames keyed by identifier onto a shared bus, so messages carry `can_id` (Bosch CAN).

checksum.description: Integrity scheme. Worth stating precisely: a mismatched checksum rule is the usual reason a first implementation is silently rejected by the device.

algorithm.description: Algorithm over the frame. 'sum8'/'sum8-mod256' is a plain 8-bit additive checksum.

scope.description: Exactly which bytes are summed, and whether it differs by direction. State this even when it seems obvious -- the Bafang BBS02 sums every preceding byte on a read response but skips the first code byte on a write request, and that asymmetry is the classic cause of rejected writes.

messages.description: The message catalogue. One entry per distinct exchange, packet shape or frame, whichever this bus uses; the `fields` array is the part every style shares.

allOf.$comment: Same rule as BLE commands: an advanced message must explain itself.

direction.description: Which way this message travels, from the host's point of view.

request.description: Bytes the host sends (request_response style). Include any payload and checksum actually required -- not every read is a bare opcode.

response.description: Expected reply prefix, where a fixed one exists. '??' marks a variable byte.

start_byte.description: Fixed leading byte identifying this packet shape (stream style), e.g. '43'.

length.description: Total frame length in bytes, including any start byte and checksum.

rate_hz.description: How many times a second this packet is emitted (stream/broadcast style).

payload_offset.description: Where `fields` offsets are measured from, when they are relative to a payload rather than the whole frame. Omit when offsets are frame-absolute. State it either way rather than leaving a reader to infer it.

fields.description: Decoded fields. Offsets are frame-absolute unless `payload_offset` says otherwise.

items.$comment: `unit` and `scale` live in $defs/number_semantics, shared with BLE `format` fields and command `parameters`, which also adds `value_offset`, `unit_source`/`unit_reference`/`unit_values` and machine-readable `values` here.

encoding.description: Value encoding in prose where an enum or code table applies, e.g. '0x1F-0x3C = 16in-30in, 0x37 = 700C'.

array_len.description: Number of consecutive same-width entries starting at `offset`. Use this for repeated per-level values instead of describing them in prose -- it is exactly the distinction between ten current limits followed by ten speed limits and ten interleaved pairs, which is the kind of thing that is otherwise got wrong silently.

writes.description: True if this message mutates device state. Note that in 'stream' style a control packet writes by existing at all -- it asserts its fields on every repetition.

advanced.description: Same meaning as on BLE commands: goes further than a typical consumer app would. A signpost, not a gate.

advanced_reason.description: Why, in the terms described for BLE commands: what changes, the realistic consequence, and how to recover.

scheduling.description:
How a device performs an action at a future time BY ITSELF, without a client being present to send it.

Worth a block of its own because the difference is invisible from the control surface and decides what an integration can promise. A client can always send an on command at 17:00 if it happens to be running; a device that stores its own schedule keeps it when the phone is asleep, the app is closed or the laptop is shut. Wemo is the worked example, and its mechanism is a SQLite database moved over SOAP in both directions.

State `supported: false` where a device has no such facility — that is an answer, and it saves the next person looking.

mechanism.description: What kind of thing the device keeps. 'on_device_rules' is a stored schedule the device evaluates against its own clock; 'countdown_timer' is a duration it counts down after being told to (the Crock-Pot's cook time), which is not the same promise; 'cloud_only' means the schedule lived in a vendor service and died with it.

runs_without_a_client.description: Whether the action still happens with nothing else on the network. The single most useful fact in this block.

applies_to.description: Which of `device.variants` (by name) the `supported` claim is evidenced for, on a spec covering a family. Omit only when the claim genuinely holds family-wide. A consumer branching on `supported` must intersect with this list: outside it the honest answer is UNKNOWN, not yes — Wemo's rules service is proven on the switch family and an open question on the appliance classes, and an unscoped true would advertise scheduling for a slow cooker nobody has scheduled.

device_clock_dependency.description: How the device knows what time it is, and what happens when it does not. A stored schedule is only as right as the clock under it, and these devices lost their time source when the vendor cloud went away.

transfer.description: How the schedule gets onto the device, as ordered steps in the same shape `setup.methods[].steps` uses.

storage.description: The stored form itself — tables, columns, and worked example rows where the schedule is a database rather than a set of parameters.

limitations.description: What the mechanism CANNOT express. This is the part a reader needs before designing a feature on top of it: Wemo's rule actions are on/off/toggle, so a scheduled Crock-Pot mode is not expressible however much the table looks like it should be.

open_questions.description: What is not established, stated so a consumer can tell inference from evidence. A schedule written from a guessed column encoding fires at the wrong time on somebody's dinner.

commands.description:
Named invocations a client can send, for devices whose control surface is not a GATT characteristic. Keyed by command name; an entity's `commands:` role map (`turn_on: plug_turn_on`) names an entry here, exactly as it names a characteristic's command on a BLE device.

The distinction from `http_endpoints`/`mqtt_topics` is what makes both blocks necessary: those catalogue the ACTIONS a device offers -- what exists, what it takes, what it returns -- while a command here is one INVOCATION of an action with its arguments already chosen. 'Turn the plug on' is SetBinaryState with BinaryState=1, and that '1' has nowhere else to live: an entity's role map carries a name, not a payload. A consumer sends one by substituting `parameters` into `arguments` and rendering through whatever request template the spec's transport block publishes.

Deliberately not `additionalProperties: false`. BLE specs (airthings-wave-family) already keep a top-level command catalogue keyed by `characteristic`/`template`/`value`, and the point of one block is that a role map resolves the same way whatever the transport underneath it is.

transport.description: How this command reaches the device. Says which of the spec's transport blocks supplies the request template and the address; absent means the spec's single declared transport. 'tcp-json' is a JSON document sent over a raw TCP socket -- the TP-Link Kasa smart-home protocol on port 9999 -- where the whole invocation is the JSON in `body`, obfuscated by the transport's cipher; there is no service, path or method to state.

service.description: Service the action belongs to, as the device names it -- a SOAP/UPnP serviceType URN such as 'urn:Belkin:service:basicevent:1'. It is also the key a client resolves the control URL by, which is why a command states the service rather than a path: published paths vary across firmware generations and the device's own service list is authoritative.

action.description: Name of the action invoked, spelled as it goes on the wire ('SetBinaryState'). Pairs with `service` to form a SOAPACTION header, and should match the `name` of the `http_endpoints` entry that documents the action's arguments and returns.

path.description: Request path, for transports that address by path rather than by service. Prefer resolving it from the device where the protocol offers a way to; state it here when the path is fixed. A `{name}` segment is a placeholder substituted from the like-named entry in `parameters`, exactly as `arguments` values are -- Roku's whole control surface is the path (`/keypress/PowerOn`), and REST-shaped APIs put per-client and per-child values there too ('/api/{username}/lights/{id}/state'); a renderer must refuse to send a path whose placeholders it cannot all fill.

method.description: HTTP method for a `transport: http` command, spelled as the wire wants it. Stated on the command -- not resolved from `http_endpoints` -- because the command is the executable half: a consumer must be able to send it without joining two blocks by name. Should agree with the `method` of the endpoint entry that documents the action; omit for transports that have no method. REST-shaped APIs reuse one path with different methods for different operations -- the Hue bridge reads a light with GET and sets it with PUT on the same resource -- so a `transport: http` command lacking `method` or `path` is declarative documentation rather than something a consumer may execute.

arguments.description: Argument name -> value, as the wire spells both. A value of '{name}' is substituted from the like-named entry in `parameters`; anything else is a literal this command has already decided (BinaryState '1' for an on command). Argument names are the device's, not ours: Wemo spells one BinaryState and the next one mode.

body.description: The literal request body this command sends, for transports whose invocation IS a document rather than a service/action or a path -- a `tcp-json` command's JSON (`{"system":{"set_relay_state":{"state":1}}}`). May contain '{name}' placeholders substituted from `parameters`, exactly as `arguments` values and `path` segments are. What `arguments` is for SOAP and `path` is for HTTP, `body` is for a JSON-over-socket protocol: the one place an invocation's chosen value has to live.

parameters.description: Values the caller supplies, keyed by the placeholder name used in `arguments`. Same role as a BLE command's `parameters`, and the same rule applies: a command is only sendable when every parameter is either owned by the control invoking it or defaulted here.

allOf.$comment: `default` and `source` are mutually exclusive because they answer the same question -- what happens when the caller supplies nothing -- with opposite instructions. `default` says substitute this constant; `source` says the real value lives on the device and a send without it must FAIL. A parameter carrying both would let a renderer quietly substitute the constant whenever the read-back fails, which on the Crock-Pot is a cleared timer (or a cooker stopped mid-run) with nothing on screen saying so. The first published version of the Wemo spec made exactly this mistake.

required.description: True for a value the CALLER supplies -- the option picked, the number chosen. Do not combine with `default` (a defaulted parameter is by definition omittable) or `source` (a read-back parameter is the client's job, not the caller's).

default.description: Constant used when the caller supplies nothing -- for protocol filler whose value genuinely is a constant. Present so a control that owns only one of an action's arguments can still send it. NOT for a value whose truth lives on the device: that is `source`, and the two are mutually exclusive -- see the sibling $comment.

source.description: Where a client obtains this value when it is not the one the user is setting. Three schemes, distinguished by prefix. 'state:<command>.<field>' (e.g. 'state:GetCrockpotState.time'): read back from the device. The case this exists for is an action that carries several settings at once: changing one means reading the others back and sending them along, and a spec that leaves that implicit produces a client which silently clears the settings it did not mean to touch. 'credential:<name>' (e.g. 'credential:username'): a per-device secret the client stored when it paired -- the Hue bridge's link-button flow issues a username that every subsequent path carries, and this scheme is how a spec says 'that stored value goes here' without pretending to know it. 'instance:<key>' (e.g. 'instance:id'): the identifier of the child currently being addressed, for commands bound by an entity with `instances:` -- the enumeration the entity's `state_command` returns supplies the ids, and this scheme names which placeholder each id fills. All three share one contract, and it is the point of the field: a `source` parameter deliberately has no `default` -- obtaining the value is PART OF THE SEND, and a renderer reaching it with no value must fail the write visibly rather than substitute anything. An unpaired client failing loudly at 'no credential:username' is correct behaviour; quietly sending without it would be a bug wearing a fallback's clothes. Consumers therefore treat `source` -- like `default` -- as satisfying the 'every blank fillable' rule when deciding whether a control is offered at all, and enforce the value's presence at send time instead.

returns.description: What the call answers with, when that is worth stating -- typically because the reply acknowledges the request rather than reporting the resulting state, which decides whether a client can use it as a reading.

example_body.description: The exact request this command produces, as bytes go out. The highest-value field here for the same reason test vectors are for crypto: it turns 'my request is rejected and I cannot tell which half is wrong' into a diff.

allOf.$comment: The button contract, enforced rather than only described: a button binds exactly one role, `press`, and carries no state binding. Without this the platform's own description is the only thing saying so, and a spec outside this repository -- which our pytest suite never sees -- could validate a button with no commands at all, or a `turn_on` a consumer has no button semantics for, and ship a control that does nothing when pressed. Stated as a conditional so every other platform is untouched.

platform.description: Home Assistant entity platform. Enum kept aligned with the mobile app; 'number' and 'select' added for devices such as the AdMore Light Bar, 'button' for momentary actions with no state to read back -- a Roku remote key is pressed, not turned on. A `button` entity binds exactly one role, `press`, whose command must have no caller-supplied blanks, and it is the one platform excused from naming a state source: statelessness is the honest description of a keypress. A `text` entity is text entry into whatever field the device has focused (a TV's search box): it binds a valued `submit` role whose command takes the one character being typed -- one send per keystroke, because the wire protocols these exist for (Roku's Lit_ key form) carry no string type -- plus an optional fixed `press` role for the deletion key. Like a button it is excused from naming a state source: the device never reports what is in its focused field.

icon.description: Material Design Icons name for this entity, as 'mdi:heat-wave'. Only worth stating when `device_class` does not already imply the right picture: a consumer draws a thermostat for device_class 'temperature' without being told, but Gerbing's heat *level* is a percentage with no device_class that says 'this warms you up'. Advisory -- a consumer that does not ship the MDI set falls back to whatever it derives from `platform`/`device_class`, so an entity must not depend on the icon to be understandable.

precision.description: Display rounding for this entity's state, as the smallest increment worth showing (0.1 = one decimal, 1.0 = whole numbers). This is a PRESENTATION rule, not a decode rule: it never changes the value, only how many digits of it are honest to print. State it when the device reports more resolution than it actually has -- a field decoded with `scale: 0.01` renders as '10.00' unless something says the last digit is noise. Distinct from `step`, which is how finely a control may be *set*.

notes.description: Free-form caveats about this entity that the structured keys cannot carry -- an unconfirmed scaling, a reading that is only valid in some device mode, a variant that lacks the sensor.

variants.description: Which of `device.variants` actually expose this entity, by name. Airthings' Wave Plus reports pressure and the Gen 1 does not, and one spec covers both -- without this a consumer draws a permanently blank tile on half the hardware. Omit when every variant has it.

unit.description: Display unit for the entity's state ('C', '%', 'km/h'). Must agree with what the bound characteristic field or command parameter declares AFTER its scale/value_offset are applied — the entity layer describes decoded values, never raw bytes. When the bound field's unit_source is 'device_setting' there is no single true value here; state the out-of-box default and let the consumer follow the field's `unit_reference`.

min.description: Smallest settable value, for platform 'number' controls — in the entity's `unit`, i.e. after the bound field's scale/value_offset, because this describes the control a user sees rather than the byte on the wire.

max.description: Largest settable value for a 'number' control, in the same decoded terms as `min`.

step.description: Control granularity for a 'number' control, in `unit` terms. Record the device's real resolution where known, not a cosmetic rounding — the difference decides whether the UI can express every state the device can hold.

min_temp.description: The `climate` platform's spelling of `min`, in the entity's `unit`. Climate entities use the temperature-named trio because that is what they are: Hotwired's heated gear declares its 0-10 heat level this way. Do not state both spellings on one entity.

max_temp.description: The `climate` platform's spelling of `max`, in the same decoded terms as `min_temp`.

temp_step.description: The `climate` platform's spelling of `step`, in `unit` terms.

state_characteristic.description: GATT characteristic this entity reads its state from.

command_characteristic.description: GATT characteristic this entity's writes go to, when that is not `state_characteristic`. Spider Farmer's grow light reads and writes different handles. It is also the explicit permission a consumer needs to write a bare value to a characteristic rather than send a named command: naming it here is the spec author saying 'this entity's writes land here', which is why an entity that omits it gets no direct-write path at all.

fallback_characteristic.description: The `command_characteristic` of an older hardware revision covered by the same spec -- Hotwired's heated gear moved from the fee0 UUID family to ffb0 and both are still in the field. Try the primary first and fall back on a device that does not expose it. NOTE: declarative. A consumer that ignores this simply does not drive the older revision; it will not mis-drive the newer one.

fallback_state_characteristic.description: The `state_characteristic` of the same older revision `fallback_characteristic` describes.

value_template.description: Jinja2 expression extracting this entity's state from a raw characteristic value, in Home Assistant's template dialect, e.g. "{{ value[3:4] | int(base=16) }}". A last resort: it says where the bytes are in a form only an HA-shaped consumer can execute, so prefer a `format:` block on the characteristic plus `state_mapping`, which says the same thing structurally and every consumer can read. NOTE: declarative -- a consumer with no Jinja engine cannot render this entity, which is why the structured route is the one to reach for.

state_field.description: Source of this entity's state on a `bus` device, as 'message_name.field_name' (e.g. 'motor_status.speed'). The bus analogue of `state_characteristic`: bus devices have no GATT characteristic to point at, so an entity binds to a decoded field of a catalogued message instead.

state_topic.description: MQTT topic or HTTP endpoint that provides entity state (for WiFi devices). Use this when the topic alone identifies the reading; when the state comes from an RPC-style call, use `state_endpoint`/`state_command`/`state_path` instead.

state_endpoint.description: HTTP endpoint the state call is made against, for WiFi devices whose API is one POST path carrying a named command rather than a REST resource per reading. Divoom's panels are the case: everything goes to `/divoom_api`, and `state_command` says which reading you asked for. The literal 'cloud' means the value is only obtainable from the vendor's cloud, not the device on the LAN -- a consumer with no cloud credentials should treat those entities as unavailable rather than broken.

state_command.description: Command name posted to `state_endpoint` to fetch this entity's state, e.g. 'Channel/GetOnOff'. Names a command in the spec's own `http_endpoints`/command vocabulary.

state_path.description: Where the reading sits inside the JSON `state_command` returns, in dotted path notation with numeric indices in brackets: 'DeviceList[0].DevicePrivateIP'. Omit when the response *is* the value.

instances.description: Declares this entity as a TEMPLATE stamped out once per child device behind a hub, rather than a single reading. A hub is one network presence fronting a population the spec cannot enumerate -- which lights exist on a Hue bridge is the owner's business, not the spec's -- so the entity describes the SHAPE of a child and this block says how a client discovers the actual children: the reply to `state_command` is a JSON object keyed by instance id ('1', '2', ...), each value one child's complete state. A client enumerates the keys, and for each one reads roles via `state_mapping` (whose dotted paths resolve INSIDE that child's object, not from the response root) and sends commands by substituting the id into the like-named `instance:` parameter of the bound commands. Enumeration and state deliberately ride one request: a hub answers for all its children at once, and per-child polling of a bridge that rate-limits is how third-party clients get themselves throttled. An entity without this block binds to exactly one reading, as ever -- consumers that predate the key see an entity whose state_mapping paths do not resolve from the root and render nothing, which is the correct degraded behaviour for a hub they do not understand.

keyed_by.description: Name of the identifier the response object is keyed by, which is also the `instance:` parameter name the bound commands substitute it into -- `keyed_by: id` pairs with 'source: instance:id'. The name is the coupling, so a spec must spell it identically in both places.

label_path.description: Dotted path, inside one child's object, to its human-facing name ('name' for a Hue light, whose owner called it 'Kitchen counter'). Optional: a client falls back to the bare instance id, which is honest but reads like a database. Same dotted-path notation as `state_mapping` values.

state_mapping.description: How this entity's state is read out of what the transport returns. Deliberately open: the useful key set differs per platform and the vocabulary is still growing, so the keys below are the ones the catalogue uses rather than a closed list. Role keys name a field of the bound characteristic's `format:` block -- `value` (the reading itself), `is_on`, `brightness`, `color_rgb`, `state`, `effect`, `rgb`, and the climate quartet `current_temperature`/`target_temperature`/`hvac_mode`/`fan_mode`. On an HTTP entity the role values are dotted JSON paths into what `state_command` returns ('state.on', 'state.bri') -- resolved from the response root, or, when the entity declares `instances:`, from inside the current child's object. `scale` is an entity-level linear factor that REPLACES the bound field's own transform rather than compounding with it -- an entity-level scale is that layer's complete statement about its value. `on_when`/`on_value` say which raw value counts as on. `options`/`states` enumerate a `select`'s choices and a device's named states. A bare integer key is a code table mapping a raw value to a label. A `<role>_fallback` key -- `value_fallback` for `value` -- is a SECOND source for that same role, for a firmware or hardware revision that reports the identical reading under a different field name: an object with `path` (resolved exactly as the role's own value is) and an optional `scale` applied to whatever `path` yields. Read the role's primary source first and fall back only when that key is absent from the reply; a consumer that ignores the key still works on current firmware, which is why this is a fallback rather than a variant split -- splitting a renamed field across two entities makes a consumer that ignores `variants` draw the tile twice. NOTE: consumers vary in what they implement; an entity should still be identifiable from `platform`/`device_class`/`unit` when a consumer understands none of these.

options_source.description: Where a `select` gets options the spec cannot enumerate, because they live on the device: Roku's installed channels are whatever the owner installed, not a table this file could keep. `command` names an `http_endpoints` entry (its method and path are the request); the response is XML, and the contract is deliberately tiny -- every element whose LOCAL NAME equals `item`, anywhere in the document, is one option; the attribute named by `value` carries the option's raw value (what the select_option command's one parameter receives); the element's own text, trimmed, is the label a user sees. An element missing the value attribute is skipped. A select carrying this key needs no static `options` table and -- uniquely among selects -- no state binding to be offered: the options ARE its surface, and `state_source` below is how it also shows which one is current.

command.description: Name of the `http_endpoints` entry to fetch, e.g. 'Installed Apps'.

item.description: Local element name matched anywhere in the response document; one element, one option.

value.description: Attribute carrying the option's raw value.

state_source.description: Where a dynamically-optioned `select` reads which option is current, in exactly `options_source`'s shape and contract: fetch the named endpoint, find the first element with `item`'s local name, read the `value` attribute -- that raw value matches an option's. An element without the attribute means no option is current (Roku's home screen reports an <app> with no id), which a consumer shows as nothing selected rather than an error. Optional on purpose: a launcher without it still launches.

command.description: Name of the `http_endpoints` entry to fetch, e.g. 'Active App'.

item.description: Local element name of the element carrying the current selection.

value.description: Attribute carrying the current raw value, matched against option values.
